passages.t: Woe to the city of blood
passages.happening:
‘Woe to the city of blood, full of lies, full of plunder, never without prey’ (verse 1). The crack of the whip, the rumble of wheels, galloping horses and bounding chariots (verse 2). Charging horsemen, flashing swords, and the dead beyond counting (verse 3). All this because of the city's harlotries, the seductive mistress of sorcery who betrays nations (verse 4).

The LORD of Hosts says he is against Nineveh. He will expose her shame to the nations and make a spectacle of her (verses 5-6). All who see her will turn away and say that Nineveh is devastated, and ask who will grieve for her. ‘Where can I find comforters for you?’ is God's last word in the speech (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The woe, hoy, was the cry raised at funerals. Prophets used it to announce judgment, as if mourning someone already as good as dead. The first lines are among the most breathless in the Bible, a rush of nouns with hardly a verb: whip, wheel, horse, chariot, horseman, sword, spear. They read like snapshots from a battlefield. These notes do not repeat the picture of the dead.

Nineveh is pictured as a harlot and a mistress of sorcery. Prostitution here is a figure for the way Assyria lured smaller nations into alliances and treaties that became traps, and sorcery points to deception and to the divination and magic for which Mesopotamia was known.

Verse 5's threat draws on the ancient practice of publicly shaming a woman, and on the humiliation of captives, who were often led away stripped. The image is deliberately harsh, and it belongs to the prophets' vocabulary of disgrace; Isaiah uses it of Babylon. The speech ends with God's own question, who will grieve for her.
passages.later: Isaiah speaks of Babylon's disgrace in the same terms (Isaiah 47:2-3). God says the same words, ‘Behold, I am against you’, at the end of chapter 2 (Nahum 2:13).
passages.hard:
How should the picture of Nineveh as a shamed woman be read?

Verse 5 pictures a city's disgrace in the language of a woman stripped and exposed. Many readers find it painful, and readers who have known abuse may find it very hard. It is a picture of an empire brought low, drawn from the prophets' vocabulary of humiliation and from the way captives were treated in that world. It is not a description of what anyone should do to a woman, and it gives no warrant for any person to shame, strip or harm a woman, or anyone.

If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: God asks who will grieve for Nineveh. Ask what kind of power ends with no one to mourn it. And ask whether there is anyone in your life who would find no comforter if you fell, because of how you have treated them.

passages.happening:
‘Are you better than Thebes, stationed by the Nile with water around her, whose rampart was the sea, whose wall was the water?’ (verse 8). Cush and Egypt were her strength, and Put and Libya her allies (verse 9). ‘Yet she became an exile; she went into captivity’ (verse 10). The verse goes on to name the cruelties done to her children and her nobles, which these notes name and do not describe.

Nineveh too will stagger and hide (verse 11). Her fortresses are like fig trees with the first ripe figs: shake them and they fall into the eater's mouth (verse 12). Her gates stand wide open to her enemies, and fire burns their bars (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Nahum calls Thebes No-Amon, the city of the god Amun. Thebes, on the Nile in upper Egypt, was one of the grandest cities of the ancient world and Egypt's religious capital for centuries. In the seventh century BC Egypt was ruled by a dynasty from Cush, south of Egypt, which is why Cush and Egypt are named as Thebes' strength. Put and Libya were peoples of North Africa allied with Egypt.

The Assyrian king Ashurbanipal invaded Egypt and sacked Thebes around 663 BC, carrying off its treasures and people, as Assyrian inscriptions record. Nahum's hearers knew that Assyria had done to Thebes exactly what verse 10 describes: exile, the killing of children, captives divided by lot, and nobles in chains. Assyria's own inscriptions and carvings record such treatment openly.

The question is a mirror. Nineveh trusted its rivers and walls as Thebes had. What Assyria did to others is coming home.
passages.later: Jeremiah and Ezekiel also spoke against Thebes, under the name No (Jeremiah 46:25; Ezekiel 30:14-16).
passages.asks: Nineveh was asked whether it was any better than the city it had destroyed. Ask whether you have judged others for what you would excuse in yourself. And ask what walls you trust that could open in a single day.

passages.t: Locusts that fly away, and an incurable wound
passages.happening:
The prophet mocks the defenders: “Draw your water for the siege; strengthen your fortresses. Work the clay and tread the mortar; repair the brick kiln!” (verse 14). But fire will devour them and the sword cut them down (verse 15). Nineveh's merchants are more than the stars, but like locusts they strip the land and fly away (verse 16). Its guards and officials are like locusts that settle on the walls on a cold day and fly off when the sun rises, and no one knows where (verse 17).

‘O king of Assyria, your shepherds slumber; your officers sleep’ (verse 18). His people are scattered on the mountains, with no one to gather them. ‘There is no healing for your injury; your wound is severe. All who hear the news of you applaud your downfall, for who has not experienced your constant cruelty?’ (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The siege preparations are real practice. A city under siege needed stored water, and its walls, largely of mud brick in Mesopotamia, needed constant repair, so defenders worked clay, trod mortar and fired bricks. Nahum tells them to do it, knowing it will fail.

The locust pictures turn twice. First the enemy will consume Nineveh like locusts. Then Nineveh's own merchants and officials are the locusts, numerous while the weather is cold and gone when the heat comes. Locusts settled on walls in the cool of the morning and flew off as the sun warmed them.

The book ends, like Jonah, with a question. Jonah ends with God asking whether he should not care about Nineveh. Nahum ends by asking who has not felt Nineveh's cruelty. When Nineveh fell in 612 BC, the nations of the region had little reason to mourn it. Within a generation the empire was gone.
passages.later: Jonah ends with God's own question about the same city: ‘So should I not care about the great city of Nineveh’ (Jonah 4:11)? Ezekiel hears God ask, ‘Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked?’ (Ezekiel 18:23).
passages.hard:
Why does the book end with applause at Nineveh's fall and no offer of mercy, when Jonah shows God sparing the same city?

The difference between Jonah and Nahum is real and deliberate. Jonah shows that God's mercy reaches even Israel's worst enemy when that enemy repents. Nahum speaks to a later time, when Nineveh's violence had gone on for generations, and it speaks to the victims rather than to the Assyrians. Some interpreters see the two books as a pair, showing both sides of what God said of himself at Sinai: he is compassionate and slow to anger, and he will by no means leave the guilty unpunished. Others stress that the applause in verse 19 comes from the nations who suffered, not from God taking pleasure in death, and they point to Ezekiel, where God asks whether he takes any pleasure in the death of the wicked.

The closing question, who has not experienced your constant cruelty, asks the reader to weigh Assyria's conduct rather than simply to rejoice. Readers who find the ending hard are in good company; the canon itself keeps Jonah and Nahum together in the one Book of the Twelve.

These notes do not gloat over Nineveh, and they do not invite anyone to. Nineveh's fall is no key for reading any people's suffering, then or now, as a punishment they deserved, and no warrant for anyone to wish destruction on a city or a people today. The book's warning is for every power that lives by cruelty, the reader's own included.
passages.asks: The last question in Nahum is who has not felt Nineveh's cruelty. Ask who has felt yours, in small ways or large. And ask what it would mean to leave the judgment of the cruel to God, while refusing to become cruel yourself.
